source.title: Iterative Averaging in the Quest for Best Test Error

record.file_problem: Text appears to contain the full paper, including appendices. No material truncation is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how iterate averaging, weight decay, optimiser, and learning-rate choices affect generalisation and related measured properties using experiments and a theoretical perturbation analysis; it does not reproduce the claim's original random-label or architecture comparisons.
record.gate_note: The paper reports outcomes for iterate averaging and its proposed adaptive variants, including held-out performance, averaging frequency, weight decay, model size association, and sharpness comparisons. Results cited from earlier papers are not extracted. In particular, the paper's comparison of sharpness measures does not test magnitude-aware sharpness as defined in V7.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares held-out performance of adaptive and SGD-family optimizers, testing V4 with different averaging, regularization and tuning recipes. It does not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness measure.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors argue that large learning rates and suitable regularization make iterate averaging effective, and that their adaptive averaging variants can outperform SGD across vision and language tasks. They also report near-monotonic late-training improvements and preliminary evidence of reduced tuning needs. Qualification is needed: default Gadam does not always beat SGD, and its strongest full-ImageNet settings sacrifice convergence speed.
record.recipe_differences: Uses iterate averaging and proposed Adam-family variants with tuned or partially tuned schedules and regularisation, rather than testing the original claim's random-label memorization, width sweep, architecture comparison, batch-size comparison, or dropout. It directly compares held-out performance across optimisers and reports associated sharpness measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Held-out outcomes vary with optimiser and averaging, weight decay, batch normalisation, learning rate and schedule, averaging frequency, and task/model. The paper reports a larger Gadam-over-AdamW improvement with batch normalisation; averaging less frequently is reported as similarly good or slightly better; larger initial learning rates can improve Gadam/GadamX while costing convergence speed.

fits_no_version.finding: SGD iterate averaging improves held-out performance relative to learning-rate decay; weight decay increases averaging benefits and prediction diversity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Iterate averaging can improve generalization, with benefits depending on regularization and learning-rate choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Batch normalization increases the benefit of Gadam over AdamW.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalization can modify the effectiveness of averaging within adaptive optimization.

fits_no_version.finding: Conventional Hessian sharpness metrics do not consistently track test accuracy across the tested VGG solutions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unscaled Hessian spectral norm, Frobenius norm and trace need not consistently predict held-out accuracy across optimizers and learning rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Averaging improvements tend to grow with parameter count across heterogeneous networks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of iterate averaging may increase with model parameter count.

record.peer_reviewed: Journal of Machine Learning Research 1 (2021), as printed in the supplied text; submission and publication metadata are marked TBD.
record.problems: Adaptive methods are not tuned as extensively as non-adaptive baselines in some CIFAR experiments; the authors specifically state AdamW results may or may not be optimal. Several comparisons are described qualitatively from figures without exact values in the text. The ImageNet table provides no uncertainty values. The sharpness comparison is limited to one architecture and lacks a clear correlation; the authors themselves say they find no clear correlation between flatness and generalisation.
record.rows_left_out: No required rows omitted. Figure-only curves without textual numerical or directional results were not reconstructed into rows; the text reports the qualitative figure findings where included.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label generalization and their coexistence.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.

A controlled comparison restricted to learning-rate and decay-schedule tuning; switching Adam to SGD; and systematic evidence that held-out differences persist despite equal or better adaptive training performance. Tuning effort is unequal, and weight decay, averaging and numerical stability also vary.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and remedies for large-batch penalties.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on dataset size or augmentation.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps among similarly fitted networks, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and retraining against random-removal controls.

missing.what: ImageNet ResNet-18: AdamW 69.92%, SGD 69.72%, Gadam 70.11% top-1 accuracy. The authors exclude this architecture from the main table because AdamW already outperforms SGD.
missing.locator: Section 7, paragraph following the numerical-stability discussion

missing.what: Missing Table 4 conditions: VGG-16 CIFAR-100 has SGD/Adam(W)/Padam(W)/Gadam/GadamX accuracies 74.15/73.26/74.56/75.73/76.85%; PRN-110 CIFAR-10 has 95.40/94.69/95.28/95.27/95.95%. Include reported uncertainties and SWA controls.

ImageNet Gadam recipe dependence: default ResNet-50 Gadam reaches 75.52%; increasing its learning rate to 0.003 reaches 76.53%; the strongest Gadam settings use learning rate 0.5 and numerical stability constant 1, sacrificing convergence speed. GadamX changes its constant to 10^-4; retaining the traditional constant gives 77.19% rather than 77.31%.

Schedule-dependent optimizer comparisons: VGG CIFAR-100 step scheduling gives SGD/AdamW/Padam 73.28/73.20/74.46%, whereas linear scheduling gives 74.15/73.26/74.56%; PRN-110 step gives 77.23/75.27/73.95%, versus linear 77.22/75.47/77.30%.
PTB Padam test perplexity is 62.15±0.12 versus ASGD 61.98±0.19, showing a much smaller adaptive disadvantage than Adam.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for the supplied versions. V7 should be marked untested, not tested_not_extracted: its defining magnitude-aware measure is absent. Mixed optimizer rows require condition-specific interpretation; their partial states summarize mixed outcomes rather than a uniformly small effect.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label memorization or natural-label coexistence experiment.
No one-hidden-layer width sweep past the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.

Does not test the specific limited-tuning comparison described by Wilson et al.; tests Adam-family methods with and without averaging against SGD-family baselines in several settings. Does not test switching from Adam to SGD.
No large-batch versus small-batch comparison or workload-dependent batch-size sweep.

Compares Hessian spectral norm, Frobenius norm, and trace against test accuracy for some VGG-16 CIFAR-100 solutions, but does not measure magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness or rank generalization gaps against norm- and margin-based measures.
No removal or retraining of memorized examples.

rows.subject: VGG-16
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; no batch normalisation or data augmentation
rows.operation_detail: Compared iterate averaging with the SGD learning-rate-drop schedule at the same point, with weight decay varied.
rows.measure: Held-out test error improvement of iterate averaging over the SGD learning-rate-drop schedule.
rows.value: IA reduces test error by a greater margin (≈ 2%) at the same point.
rows.uncertainty: 10 seeds are reported for the weight-decay comparison; no uncertainty value stated for this specific comparison.
rows.note: The text describes an improvement over the learning-rate equivalent; exact plotted values are not supplied.
rows.check: Compares SGD averaging with SGD learning-rate decay, not adaptive optimization with SGD. The reported averaging improvement does not test V4.

rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; no batch normalisation or data augmentation
rows.operation_detail: Compared iterate averaging with sharp learning-rate decay over multiple weight-decay settings.
rows.measure: Held-out test error and margin of IA improvement over the sharp-decay schedule.
rows.baseline: Sharp learning-rate decay at the same weight-decay value
rows.value: IA improves over the SGD learning-rate equivalent for all tested weight-decay values; the improvement margin increases with regularisation.
rows.uncertainty: 10 seeds; no numerical error bar stated for this figure.
rows.note: The paper gives the direction and trend, not exact test-error values in the text.
rows.check: Weight-decay dependence of SGD averaging benefits does not measure any supplied version.

rows.subject: VGG-16
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; no batch normalisation or data augmentation
rows.operation_detail: Compared iterate averaging and sharp learning-rate decay across weight-decay strengths.
rows.measure: Average symmetric KL-divergence between IA solutions.
rows.value: Greater weight decay gives greater solution diversity.
rows.note: This measures solution diversity, not held-out performance directly; recorded because it is a measured property accompanying the regularisation/generalisation comparison.
rows.check: Prediction diversity between iterates is not an adaptive-versus-SGD held-out performance comparison.

rows.subject: PreResNet-110
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation error for SGD-IA, Gadam, and Adam-IA.

conditions.value: same L2 regularisation (0.0001) for the comparison

rows.value: Adam-IA has a significantly smaller error drop than SGD-IA; Gadam has a larger drop and outperforms SGD-IA.
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative comparison; exact figure values are not stated.
rows.check: Combines different outcomes and should be split: final averaging reduces validation error by 5.8 percentage points for Adam-IA, 9.0 for SGD-IA and 11.9 for Gadam. A smaller averaging-induced drop alone does not establish worse final performance; the text explicitly establishes Gadam outperforming SGD-IA.

rows.subject: PreResNet-110
rows.operation_detail: Compared iterate-averaged Adam with AdamW-based Gadam using decoupled weight decay.

conditions.value: AdamW decoupled weight decay 0.25 for Gadam

rows.measure: Validation error change at the final iterate-average point.
rows.value: Gadam has a greater validation-error drop than Adam-IA, even outperforming SGD-IA.
rows.note: The authors attribute the improvement alongside increased solution diversity.
rows.check: Relevant to recovery through decoupled weight decay combined with averaging. Include the SGD-IA comparator explicitly; the Adam-IA comparison alone would not establish recovery relative to SGD.

rows.subject: VGG-16
rows.operation_detail: Compared AdamW, Gadam, and GadamX with and without batch normalisation.
rows.measure: Validation error improvement of Gadam over AdamW.
rows.value: The margin of Gadam improvement over AdamW is much larger with BN.
rows.note: The comparison is qualitative in the text; exact values are not stated.
rows.check: Compares two adaptive recipes and their sensitivity to batch normalization without an SGD comparator.

rows.subject: ResNeXt-29
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimisers with and without iterate averaging.

rows.note: Gadam and GadamX are IA-based adaptive variants; Adam(W) is lower than SGD, while Gadam and GadamX exceed it. Table reports means over three runs.
rows.check: Split by optimizer: Adam(W) trails SGD, whereas Padam(W), Gadam and GadamX exceed SGD. Gadam remains below SWA. The uncertainties correspond to SGD, SWA, Adam(W), Padam(W), Gadam and GadamX, including the baseline.

rows.subject: VGG-16
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimisers with and without iterate averaging.
rows.uncertainty: Reported as ± values with each result.
rows.note: The adaptive methods without averaging are below SGD; Gadam exceeds Adam(W), while GadamX exceeds SGD.

rows.operation_detail: Compared optimisers with and without iterate averaging.
rows.uncertainty: Reported as ± values with each result.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimisers on ImageNet; Gadam and GadamX use iterate averaging.

conditions.value: comparisons include step and linear schedules as indicated in optimiser names

rows.note: AdamW is below SGD; Gadam and GadamX are above SGD. No uncertainty reported in this table.
rows.check: AdamW trails SGD and Ranger approximately matches it; Gadam and GadamX exceed it. Table 3 Gadam uses substantially altered numerical stability and learning-rate settings, not the default Gadam recipe.

rows.subject: ResNet-101
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimisers on ImageNet; Gadam and GadamX use iterate averaging.

conditions.value: comparisons include step and linear schedules as indicated in optimiser names

rows.note: AdamW and Ranger are below SGD; averaging-based Gadam and GadamX are above it.
rows.check: AdamW and Ranger trail SGD, while tuned Gadam and GadamX exceed it. Identify the altered numerical stability and learning-rate settings used for these results.

rows.subject: 3-layer LSTM
rows.operation_detail: Compared adaptive and non-adaptive optimisers on PTB; Gadam and GadamX use averaging.
rows.uncertainty: Reported as ± values with each result.
rows.note: On this language benchmark, Adam has worse test perplexity than ASGD but Gadam and GadamX have lower perplexity.
rows.check: Constant-schedule Adam trails ASGD, whereas averaged adaptive variants outperform ASGD. For PTB, Gadam uses Adam with L2 regularization, not AdamW with decoupled weight decay.

rows.subject: 3-layer LSTM
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimiser variants under scheduled language-model training.
rows.note: The authors state Gadam and GadamX outperform the tested variants without careful learning-rate scheduling; Gadam is better than scheduled Adam, while Adam's comparison with NT-ASGD is not uniform.
rows.check: Scheduled Adam outperforms NT-ASGD, consistent with V4's language-model exception. Gadam/GadamX values are reused from Table 10, not new scheduled runs; NT-ASGD is weaker than manually triggered ASGD under this 200-epoch budget.

rows.subject: VGG-16
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; no batch normalisation
rows.operation_detail: Compared AdamW and Gadam with sharpness metrics and held-out accuracy at different terminal learning rates.
rows.measure: Test accuracy and Hessian spectral norm, Frobenius norm, and trace.
rows.baseline: AdamW: 69.43 test accuracy; spectral norm 62; Frobenius norm 9.3E−4; trace 4.7E−5
rows.note: These are sharpness-related measurements, but do not measure the magnitude-aware perturbation criterion in V7; V7 is therefore marked tested_not_extracted.
rows.check: Within-adaptive-family comparisons and unscaled Hessian metrics do not test V4 or V7. The omitted parenthetical values are final-iterate controls at the same learning rates.

rows.subject: VGG-16
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; no batch normalisation
rows.operation_detail: Compared SGD and SWA with sharpness metrics and held-out accuracy at different terminal learning rates.
rows.measure: Test accuracy and Hessian spectral norm, Frobenius norm, and trace.
rows.baseline: SGD: 71.64 test accuracy; spectral norm 4.40; Frobenius norm 1.2E−5; trace 4.7E−6
rows.note: The authors state that averaging lowers curvature but they find no clear correlation between flatness and generalisation.
rows.check: SGD-versus-SWA comparisons do not test V4, and conventional Hessian metrics do not test V7's magnitude-aware perturbation criterion.

rows.subject: VGG-16
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; no batch normalisation
rows.operation_detail: Related IA performance improvement over base optimiser to model parameter count.

conditions.value: CIFAR datasets and ImageNet as discussed in the paper

rows.measure: Association between number of parameters and test improvement from IA.
rows.value: Improvement closely follows a linear trend with number of parameters; authors describe a positive relationship.
rows.note: The text reports a trend but no numeric values or model-by-model parameter counts here; it is a size association, not a test of V2's width claim.
rows.check: The subject spans multiple architectures, not VGG-16 alone. Appendix D.3 also incorporates cited results, which must be separated from this study's results. Averaging benefit versus parameter count is not V2's width sweep beyond interpolation.

relationships.condition: Unaveraged Adam-family baselines on ResNeXt CIFAR-100, ImageNet-32, PRN-110 CIFAR-100 and deeper ImageNet ResNets
relationships.reason: Adam(W) trails SGD: 80.16 versus 81.47, 55.51 versus 61.33, 75.47 versus 77.22, and 74.04/74.48 versus 75.63/77.37 top-1 accuracy (R7-R9, R11-R13); tuning also includes weight decay.
relationships.display_finding: Reported image-classification accuracy favored SGD over the unaveraged Adam-family baselines despite weight-decay tuning, but these comparisons remain unverified.

relationships.condition: Partially adaptive optimizers and weak image-classification differences
relationships.reason: Padam exceeds SGD on ResNeXt and approximately matches it on the recorded CIFAR VGG/PRN settings; VGG CIFAR-10 Adam(W)'s deficit is only 0.24 percentage points with overlapping reported variability (R7, R10, R11).
relationships.display_finding: Reported Padam parity or advantages over SGD and a small VGG Adam(W) deficit remain unverified.

relationships.condition: Adaptive optimizers combined with averaging and suitable regularization or reduced adaptivity
relationships.reason: Gadam recovers or exceeds SGD in several settings and GadamX exceeds SGD throughout R7-R13; Gadam still trails SGD on ImageNet-32, so recovery depends on recipe and workload.
relationships.display_finding: Reported recovery with Gadam and advantages with GadamX remain unverified, with Gadam still trailing SGD on ImageNet-32.

relationships.condition: PTB LSTM with constant schedules and a manually triggered ASGD baseline
relationships.reason: Adam has worse test perplexity than ASGD, 63.16 versus 61.98, under the reported 200-epoch recipe (R14).
relationships.display_finding: Reported test perplexity favored manually triggered ASGD over Adam under the stated training recipe, but the comparison remains unverified.

relationships.condition: PTB LSTM with adaptive averaging or scheduled Adam
relationships.reason: Gadam/GadamX beat ASGD at 58.77/60.45 versus 61.98; scheduled Adam reaches 61.51 and beats NT-ASGD's 64.73, showing dependence on averaging, scheduling and the SGD comparator (R14-R15).
relationships.display_finding: Reported perplexity advantages for Gadam, GadamX, and scheduled Adam over their averaged SGD comparators remain unverified.

relationships.reason: The text reports AdamW at 69.92% versus SGD at 69.72%, and Gadam at 70.11%; this small opposite-direction comparison is omitted from the rows and explicitly excluded from the main table.
relationships.display_finding: Reported small accuracy advantages for AdamW and Gadam over SGD remain unverified.

relationships.reason: Beyond R12, the text reports default Gadam at 75.52%, below SGD's 75.63%; raising its learning rate gives 76.53%, while the strongest settings sacrifice convergence speed. These recipe-dependent results need rows.
relationships.display_finding: Reported improvement from raising Gadam's learning rate remains unverified, with the strongest settings also sacrificing convergence speed.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Adam-family baselines generally trail SGD, but the proposed averaging-based adaptive variants recover or exceed SGD in many comparisons; some Gadam results remain below SGD, including WRN-28-10 ImageNet-32 accuracy (R7-R13).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Adam has worse test perplexity than ASGD, while Gadam and GadamX achieve lower perplexity; this benchmark and recipe do not establish a general adaptive-optimizer disadvantage (R14-R15).
